meta.title: ProxMenux Monitor — Dashboard: Settings tab | ProxMenux Documentation
meta.description: The Settings tab controls the Monitor language, navigation order, dashboard preferences, health thresholds and exclusions, notifications, AI and the post-install optimization inventory.

header.title: Dashboard: Settings tab
header.description: Monitor language, navigation order, dashboard preferences, monitoring exclusions, notifications, AI configuration and the live ProxMenux optimization inventory.

intro.title: Where each setting actually lives
intro.body: The Settings tab is a single surface for several distinct concerns: how the dashboard renders, what gets watched by the Health Monitor, how alerts go out, and what ProxMenux has already changed on the host. Cards that have their own deep documentation page link out rather than duplicating content here — Settings is the entry point, not the manual.

interfaceLanguage.heading: Interface Language
interfaceLanguage.intro: Choose the language used by the web Monitor. The change is applied immediately to the current interface; it does not restart the service and does not alter the language used by ProxMenux shell menus.
items: ProxMenux Monitor currently offers English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, Slovak and Swedish.
On the first visit, the Monitor uses the browser language when it is supported; otherwise it falls back to English.
Changing the selection updates the page language and synchronizes other open tabs from the same browser profile.
If a translated key is missing, only that text falls back to English instead of rendering a broken placeholder.
interfaceLanguage.scopeBody: The selection is stored in localStorage under proxmenux-ui-language. It is therefore specific to this browser profile and device, not a node-wide setting. Each operator can choose a different Monitor language.

navigationOrder.heading: Navigation order
navigationOrder.intro: Use this card to arrange the seven top-level navigation slots: Overview, Apps, VMs & LXCs, Node, Backup, Terminal and Admin. Press Edit, drag the rows, then save the result.
items: Mouse dragging starts on press. Touch uses a short 250 ms long-press so normal scrolling is not mistaken for a reorder.
The grouped Node and Admin entries move as complete units; their internal pages keep their canonical order.
The mobile menu follows the same saved order.
Restore default resets the draft order. Save to make the reset permanent.
A new top-level tab introduced by a future release is appended to an existing custom order rather than deleting the user's arrangement.
navigationOrder.landingTitle: The first item becomes the landing tab
navigationOrder.landingBody: The first saved slot is what the Monitor opens after loading. If Node is first, the landing page is Storage; if Admin is first, it is System Logs. The order is stored only in this browser under proxmenux-nav-order, so different devices can use different workflows.

networkUnits.heading: Network Units
networkUnits.imageAlt: Network Units card with Network Unit Display dropdown set to Bytes
networkUnits.imageCaption: Choose between bits per second and bytes per second for every network rate displayed in the dashboard.
networkUnits.body: Choose how network throughput is displayed across the dashboard: bits per second (Mbps / Gbps) or bytes per second (MB/s / GB/s). Bits is the default because it's what NIC vendors and ISPs label their products with; bytes is what most file-transfer tools report. The setting affects every chart, badge and tooltip that shows network rate — applied immediately, no reload needed.

health.heading: Health Monitor
health.intro: The card surfaces the per-category Suppression Duration setting — once an alert is dismissed, how long before the scanner is allowed to re-fire it. Each of the ten Health Monitor categories (CPU, Memory, Storage, Disks, Network, VMs, PVE Services, Logs, Updates, Security) has its own dropdown with these values:
items: 24 h — default for most transient categories.
72 h — for events you want a few days of silence on.
168 h (1 week) and 720 h (1 month) — periodic checks.
8760 h (1 year) — effectively "quiet for the foreseeable future".
-1 — permanent silence until you re-enable it manually.
Custom hours — any integer if you need an in-between value.
health.imageAlt: Settings → Health Monitor card with the per-category suppression dropdowns and the Active Suppressions section
health.imageCaption: Health Monitor card — the per-category dropdowns set defaults for new dismisses; the Active Suppressions section below lists every alert currently silenced and lets you revert them.
health.editBody: The card is read-only by default. Click Edit in the top-right of the card to enable the dropdowns and the Re-enable buttons. Save commits every pending change (suppression-duration changes and queued re-enables) in a single batch; Cancel discards them all. The Save button only activates when there is at least one pending change.
health.activeIntro: Below the suppression-duration dropdowns, the Active Suppressions section lists every alert that is currently silenced — both time-limited dismisses (24 h, 7 days, custom windows) and Permanent ones. Each row shows:
activeItems: A coloured badge — Permanent (amber) or a countdown such as 24h remaining / 7d remaining (blue).
The alert identifier, normalized for readability (e.g. pve_storage_full_PBS-Cloud → PVE Storage Full: PBS-Cloud).
Category, severity and the timestamp the alert was dismissed.
A Re-enable button (active only in Edit mode) that queues the alert to be un-acknowledged on the next Save.
health.activeReenableBody: Clicking Re-enable in Edit mode marks the row in green and strikes its identifier — it is queued but not yet applied. Click again on the same row to Undo the queue. When you press Save, every queued re-enable fires POST /api/health/un-acknowledge in parallel and the affected rows disappear from the list. If the underlying condition is still present and the category supports re-firing, the alert reappears in the Health Monitor's Active list on the next scan cycle.
health.activePermanentNote: Permanent dismisses (alerts dismissed with Permanently from the Health Monitor modal, or those whose category default is set to -1) can only be reverted from here. The dashboard modal does not expose an un-dismiss button for them — the Active Suppressions panel is the single audit log + revert UI.
health.activeAutoRefreshBody: The list refreshes automatically when you dismiss or un-dismiss an alert from the Health Monitor modal (via an in-browser event), when the browser tab regains focus, and on visibility change. You do not need to reload the page after dismissing an alert from the dashboard.
health.calloutTitle: Full semantics live in the Health Monitor page
health.calloutBody: The escalation rules (when a re-fire becomes critical), the auto-resolve behaviour for events whose underlying device disappears, and the difference between dismissed and resolved — all documented under <link>Health Monitor → Dismissing alerts and the Suppression Duration</link>. This card just exposes the per-category dropdowns and the Active Suppressions panel.

thresholds.heading: Health Monitor Thresholds
thresholds.intro: The previous card sets how long to stay quiet after a dismiss; this one sets the value at which an alert is raised. Most threshold-based checks have adjustable Warning and Critical values. The table below explains exceptions such as the combined swap rule.
thresholds.whatForIntro: Defaults that ship with ProxMenux are sane for the average Proxmox host, but every environment has its own envelope:
whatForItems: A small homelab with a single-disk SSD may want to page earlier on capacity (75 / 90 %) to leave room for snapshots.

Memory thresholds should reflect the host’s memory measurements and workload. Ceph redundancy alone does not justify relaxing memory warnings, and high ZFS ARC usage must not be confused with an unreclaimable working set.

Choose drive-temperature thresholds using the drive’s specifications and observed operating conditions. Passive versus forced-air cooling alone does not determine a universally lower or higher safe limit.
A heavily-virtualized host that pegs CPU during builds should not page on every 80 % spike, but must still alert on sustained pressure.
thresholds.whatForOutro: Supported threshold changes take effect on the next scan. The Health Monitor reads /usr/local/share/proxmenux/health_thresholds.json each cycle without a restart. Selected widgets, including disk temperature, use these values; some capacity bars retain separate visual cutoffs.
thresholds.coloursTitle: Status colours: how Warning and Critical render in the dashboard
thresholds.coloursIntro: Widgets that use the configured Warning/Critical pair follow the three-state classification below. Some visual indicators, including the PVE storage capacity bars, use their own cutoffs; do not infer a Health Monitor alert solely from their colour.

colourRows.meaning: Normal operating range. No alert fires.
Warning state. The Health Monitor fires a WARNING-severity event; notifications respect the channel filters and Quiet Hours.
Critical state. The Health Monitor raises a CRITICAL event, which bypasses Quiet Hours. Channel category/event settings still apply; delivery also depends on the channel being available.

thresholds.sectionsIntro: These are the values ProxMenux ships with — the recommended baseline. They're what you see on a fresh host until you override anything. Sections are ordered top-to-bottom from compute → heat → storage capacity so reading down moves from concrete (current load) to accumulated state (free space).

thresholdRows.gates: Sustained-load alert when CPU averages above the threshold for the scan window.
Swap CRITICAL requires both swap usage above 80 % and available RAM below 15 %, sustained across the detector’s samples. Used swap alone does not trigger this rule.
CPU package / core temperature reading from lm-sensors.
HDD temperature. The defaults are 60 °C Warning and 65 °C Critical; these are monitoring defaults, not a universal manufacturer limit. Check the specific drive model’s specifications.
SATA SSDs in 2.5-inch or M.2 formats. This class uses 70/75 °C monitoring defaults; actual temperature limits depend on the drive model.
NVMe temperature. The class uses 80/85 °C monitoring defaults. Controller throttling temperatures vary by model and are not universally 85 °C.
SAS temperature. This class uses 55 °C Warning and 65 °C Critical. These are monitoring defaults, not proof of a cooling fault at 55 °C or a universal manufacturer limit.
Capacity of / and every host mountpoint (/var/lib/vz, /mnt/*…).
Per-container root disk, evaluated against the rootfs size from PVE.
Capacity of mountpoints inside running CTs (mp0, mp1, NFS, bind mounts). Excludes rootfs.
Only PVE storages of type LVM, LVM-thin, ZFS-pool, RBD, CephFS and PBS. Directory, NFS and CIFS storages are covered by the host disk-space row.
ZFS pools at host level — independent of PVE registration.

thresholds.defaultsBody: The backend exposes a merged view: every section starts from the ProxMenux defaults (the values you see when the host is fresh) and you override only the knobs you care about. The card shows the effective value — the override if you set one, otherwise the default. A Reset button wipes every override and goes back to defaults across all sections at once.
thresholds.validationBody: Saving validates values against each field’s allowed range and rejects Critical below Warning. The interface shows validation errors, and the backend validates API requests again before persisting changes.

lxcDetection.heading: LXC Update Detection
lxcDetection.imageAlt: LXC Update Detection card with a single switch — when enabled, the Monitor periodically scans running Debian/Ubuntu/Alpine LXC containers for pending package updates.
lxcDetection.imageCaption: The toggle for the periodic apt list --upgradable / apk list -u scan across every running CT. Default is ON. The matching notification toggle in Notifications → Services only appears while detection is enabled.
lxcDetection.intro: A dedicated toggle for the LXC update scan, sitting between the Health Monitor Thresholds and the Notifications card. When ON, ProxMenux walks every running CT on the host and queries the in-container package manager for pending updates; results land in the Hardware tab badge counts and feed the lxc_updates_available notification. When OFF, the scan stops entirely (no pct exec calls) and any existing LXC entries in managed_installs.json are purged immediately, so the dashboard and the /api/managed-installs endpoint stop reporting LXC update state without waiting for the next 24h cycle.
lxcDetection.whatRunsIntro: For each CT in running state with a supported package manager:
whatRunsItems: Metadata freshness. If the in-container apt/apk metadata cache is older than 24 hours, a refresh is attempted first (apt-get update -qq on Debian/Ubuntu, apk update on Alpine), with a 60 s timeout. If it fails, listing still uses the available cache; results may therefore be stale.
Listing. Then ProxMenux runs apt list --upgradable / apk list -u and parses the output into a structured count plus a sample of the top package names.
Per-CT dedup. A fingerprint built from count, security-count and the sorted top names is stored so a stable set of pending updates doesn't re-notify daily, while a meaningfully different set does.
lxcDetection.selfUpdateTitle: CTs that self-update outside apt may legitimately report 0
lxcDetection.selfUpdateBody: Detection only covers the in-container package manager. Software updated outside apt, such as a configured plexupdate job or Docker images fetched with docker pull, is outside that count. Zero apt updates does not prove that every application is current. The same CT’s base system can still have package updates detected by the scan.
lxcDetection.refreshBody: Long-running CTs can have stale apt metadata if nobody runs apt update. Then apt list --upgradable can miss newer updates. ProxMenux attempts a refresh when the metadata is older than 24 hours and skips it when the cache was refreshed more recently.
lxcDetection.toggleBody: The lxc_updates_available per-channel notification toggle in Notifications → Services only renders while detection is enabled. When you turn detection OFF, that row disappears from every channel's category list — but its stored preference is preserved in the DB, so re-enabling detection brings the toggle back at the value it had before.
lxcDetection.purgeTitle: What gets purged when you disable detection
lxcDetection.purgeBody: Turning the switch OFF immediately removes every type=lxc entry from /usr/local/share/proxmenux/managed_installs.json. LXC update counts in the VMs & LXCs tab clear on the next dashboard refresh. Turning it back ON repopulates the registry on the next detection cycle, or sooner with a manual API refresh.

storageExclusions.heading: Remote Storage Exclusions
storageExclusions.imageAlt: Remote Storage Exclusions card listing PBS-Cloud, PBS and PBS2 storages with Health and Alerts toggles per row
storageExclusions.imageCaption: Per-storage Health and Alerts toggles. Storages with both toggles off stop counting against the Health Monitor and stop generating notifications — but still render on the Storage tab marked as excluded.
storageExclusions.intro: Mark Proxmox-managed storages (NFS / CIFS / PBS / Ceph / iSCSI / etc.) as excluded from monitoring. Two independent toggles per storage:
items: Health — when off, the storage stops contributing to the Storage category of the Health Monitor. Useful for archive volumes that are intentionally offline most of the time or remote backup targets only powered up on schedule.
Alerts — when off, alerts about this storage no longer go out through configured channels, even if Health checks remain enabled. Useful when you want the dashboard view but not the notifications.
storageExclusions.outro: Excluded storages still render on the Storage tab with a purple excluded badge so the entry doesn't silently disappear from your inventory. State is persisted in the excluded_storages SQLite table.

interfaceExclusions.heading: Network Interface Exclusions
interfaceExclusions.imageAlt: Network Interface Exclusions card listing vmbr0, vmbr1, vmbr2, bond0 and eno1 with Health and Alerts toggles per interface
interfaceExclusions.imageCaption: Same shape as Storage Exclusions — per-interface Health and Alerts toggles. Each row shows the interface, type badge (bridge / bond / physical), the IP and the link speed.
interfaceExclusions.intro: Same shape as Storage Exclusions but for network interfaces. Per interface: exclude from Health checks and / or exclude from notifications. Typical use cases:
items: An intentionally-down spare bridge.
A NIC that was physically removed but is still referenced in /etc/network/interfaces.
A VLAN sub-interface used only during maintenance windows.
A management bridge with known, repeated link-state changes during maintenance.
interfaceExclusions.outro: State is persisted in the excluded_interfaces SQLite table. Same purple excluded badge on the Network tab so excluded interfaces stay visible.

notifications.heading: Notifications & AI
notifications.body1: This section of the Settings tab is where ProxMenux Monitor notifications and the AI rewriter are turned on. Pressing Enable Notifications starts the dispatch background thread, registers a Proxmox VE webhook target on the host so PVE-emitted events flow into the same pipeline, and unfolds the channel form so you can connect Telegram, Discord, Email, Gotify and the rest. The AI rewriter sits inside the same panel as a collapsible advanced section.
notifications.body2: Both surfaces have a lot of moving parts — channels, per-event toggles, Rich messages, the Display Name, the dispatch pipeline (dedup, cooldown, aggregation, quiet hours), the PVE webhook integration, AI providers, prompt modes — and live on their own dedicated pages rather than being repeated here:
items: <notifLink>Notifications</notifLink> — channel walk-throughs (Telegram, Discord, Gotify, Email + Gmail / Microsoft app passwords, ntfy, Slack, Teams, generic webhook), per-event categories, Rich messages, Display Name, dispatch pipeline, PVE webhook integration, history and API.

<aiLink>AI Assistant</aiLink> — providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Groq, OpenRouter, Ollama), model selection, prompt modes (default / custom), output language, per-channel detail levels and AI suggestions.

optimizations.heading: ProxMenux Optimizations
optimizations.intro: An inventory of post-install optimizations recorded by ProxMenux on the host. Options from Automated post-install and Customizable post-install register their application in /usr/local/share/proxmenux/installed_tools.json. The Monitor reads that registry for this card. A recorded entry is not a fresh check that every underlying setting remains unchanged.
optimizations.imageAlt: ProxMenux Optimizations card with grid of installed tools, each row showing a green dot, tool name and version. Examples include APT IPv4 Force, Bashrc Customization, Fastfetch, Log2ram SSD Protection, Memory Settings Optimization, Setting persistent network interfaces, System Limits Increase, APT Language Skip, Entropy Generation haveged with Legacy badge, Kernel Panic Configuration, Logrotate Optimization, Network Optimizations, Subscription Banner Removal, VFIO IOMMU Passthrough — 14 active total
optimizations.imageCaption: The card lists every active optimization with its name, version, a coloured dot and an orange 14 active counter at the top right. Tools whose source is reachable are clickable.
dotsItems: Green dot — a registered optimization that is not marked legacy and has no available update indicated. Click the row when source code is available.

Amber dot + legacy badge — a registered optimization whose script was renamed or replaced. Its preserved source opens in legacy mode with an amber accent. This does not revalidate the current host configuration.
optimizations.clickBody: Clicking a tool opens a modal with its mapped bash function and script name (auto_post_install.sh or customizable_post_install.sh). Current tools are extracted from files on the host; legacy tools can use preserved source. Syntax highlighting and Copy help inspect the code. This is not a guaranteed snapshot of the exact code that ran at installation time.
optimizations.detailAlt: Tool source code modal for APT IPv4 Force showing the bash function force_apt_ipv4 from customizable_post_install.sh version 1.0 with syntax-highlighted code that configures /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99-force-ipv4 with Acquire ForceIPv4 true, registers the tool and emits a translate APT IPv4 configuration completed message
optimizations.detailCaption: Source modal for APT IPv4 Force — exact force_apt_ipv4() function from customizable_post_install.sh v1.0, with syntax highlighting and a one-click Copy.
optimizations.whyBody: ProxMenux can change kernel parameters, repository settings, networking, log rotation and GPU passthrough. Review the recorded optimizations before adding manual changes, especially when another administrator set up the host. The card shows registry entries and available source; it does not audit every live setting or preserve an exact execution history.
optimizations.updatesBody: When a post-install optimization gets a newer version on disk than the one currently registered on the host, the card shows an "Updates available" banner at the top with the count and an Apply button. Clicking Apply opens a per-optimization picker (the same one available from the Post-Install menu's Apply available updates entry). Pick which optimizations to lift; ProxMenux re-runs the corresponding function and refreshes the version in the registry. When everything is current the banner disappears.
optimizations.updatesAlt: ProxMenux Optimizations card with an Updates available banner at the top — count of pending updates plus an Apply button that opens the per-optimization picker
optimizations.updatesCaption: The banner only renders when at least one optimization has a newer version on disk. See <link>Apply Available Updates</link> for the full update flow and the Path-A equivalent in the shell menu.
optimizations.revertBody: To undo an optimization, use the corresponding Uninstall Optimizations option in the ProxMenux Scripts menu. Uninstalling removes its entry from installed_tools.json, so the card stops listing it on the next refresh.

rows.source: Browser preference proxmenux-ui-language, initially derived from the browser locale when no saved choice exists.
Browser preference proxmenux-nav-order; it also determines the landing tab.
Persisted in the dashboard's SQLite settings table.
Per-category suppression durations in the Health DB.
Reads /usr/local/share/proxmenux/installed_tools.json, written by register_tool calls inside the post-install scripts.
Extracts the mapped bash function from auto_post_install.sh or customizable_post_install.sh on the host; legacy tools can use preserved source.
